transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2027-09-20
- Start: 16:00 PT
- Duration: 58 minutes
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood Product), Aisha (SlateBio Head of Platform), Liam (SRE), Nora (ML Lead), Samir (Security)

Summary: quick product-led walk through of the Console 'Ops Debugger' and Forensics mode. Customer concerned about intermittent high latency and occasional hallucinations in prod, wants to see request logs, trace stitching, and how to debug fallback/cached responses.

[00:00] Maya Thompson: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros, um, i'm maya with Redwood, and diego is our solutions engineer who will drive most of the console demo. priya is on product to jump in on roadmap Qs. aisha, do you want to intro the team?

[00:12] Aisha Rahman: yeah sure thanks maya. i'm aisha, head of platform at slatebio. liam is our SRE, nora leads ML infra, and samir is security. main ask is, we had a few inference regressions that we couldn't triage — request ids were missing, and our own logs didn't correlate to model fallbacks. curious how redwood's console can stitch request traces, and also our compliance folks want to see audit trails.

[00:35] Diego Alvarez: great thanks. quick agenda: we'll show the Request Path Map, Trace Stitcher, the Replay Sandbox that replays requests through a safe environment, and then cover how the Ops Debugger surfaces KV-cache misses and fallback traces.

[01:02] (screen share starts)
[01:15] Diego Alvarez: okay pulling up the console. top left here is the request timeline view — you can filter by request id, model variant, and severity. i'm going to search for the sample id liam shared, 7cd9f1... doesn't fully match, lemme try the prefix.

[01:42] Liam Chen: quick note, sorry, the ids in our logs might get truncated by our logging agent, so we included both a short and full id.

[02:00] Diego Alvarez: got it — found a match. zooming in, you can see sub-spans: router -> cache lookup -> model call -> postprocess. the Trace Stitcher aligns timestamps from SDK instrumentation and the Redwood tracing hooks to build a single timeline. you'll notice at 00:14:22 there's a KV lookup followed by a cache miss, then a model fallback to a smaller quantized variant.

[02:35] Nora Patel: can the stitcher merge traces when the client and server times are skewed? we see clock drift across regions.

[02:48] Diego Alvarez: yes, we run a drift normalization — approximate align using request arrival timestamps and sequence numbers. sometimes names get weird in the capture though, like our auto-parser labeled your VPC NAT gateway as 'VPC-nat-2b' which might not map to your internal name — that's expected fuzziness.

[03:10] Maya Thompson: small aside, folks, a lot of auto-transcription or auto-parse will mislabel product strings — for example, we sometimes see 'Redwood Dedicate' or 'Reedwood' in auto text, just ignore that.

[03:25] Diego Alvarez: back to the trace, the interesting bit is the KV-cache miss waterfall: you can see the first cache lookup hits local LRU, then a distributed cache miss triggers a synchronous fetch that adds ~120ms, and then the model fallback path fires because the primary model exceeded a per-request latency SLO. the console flags that as a 'fallback confidence' event.

[04:00] Samir Gupta: from a security perspective, where are these traces stored? do we keep PII or raw request payloads? we need to know retention and encryption.

[04:15] Priya Nair: good question. for hosted customers we provide configurable retention plus redaction rules; for Private deployments we let you control persistence — logs can be shipped to your S3, or kept behind your KMS with envelope encryption. we also support HSM KMS key wrapping for customers that require hardware key control.

[04:42] Aisha Rahman: and audit logs for admin actions? we need an immutable trail for compliance.

[04:50] Maya Thompson: yes, audit logs are part of the enterprise package — they record console access, model rollouts, who triggered replays, and those logs are tamper-evident and exportable to your SIEM. we'll include the SOC2 summary in the follow-up.

[05:10] (Diego clicks into Replay Sandbox)
[05:22] Diego Alvarez: the Replay Sandbox — you can select a historical request and replay it against the same model config or a canary variant. important for you to reproduce the exact sequence: we capture prefix KV cache state, request meta, and simulated LLM env to avoid hitting prod models. you can run side-by-side comparisons of outputs.

[05:55] Nora Patel: do replays consume tokens / bill? we need to know cost impact for a batch of 5k replays.

[06:10] Diego Alvarez: replays execute in a controlled environment that charges at a bench rate — it's not free, but we can limit concurrency and set a cap. for pilot runs we usually offer discounted bench credits.

[06:28] Liam Chen: i want to see how rerouting works if capacity is constrained. last incident the app silently fell back to a smaller model and we didn't realize.

[06:42] Diego Alvarez: yes. open the routing policy section — here you can define rules: prefer 'redwood-hosted-larger' with a timeout of 250ms, fallback to 'redwood-compact-quant' with lower cost. the console shows both the routing decision and the output delta with a confidence metric so you can flag quality regressions.

[07:10] (Diego opens an error case)
[07:22] Diego Alvarez: here's an example error path — model call times out, runtime returns an error code 504, console surfaces the stack with the token-level latency heatmap. you can also expand the decoder logs to see if token generation stalled. sometimes the cause is kernel thrash on the serving GPU or a KV cache lock.

[07:50] Aisha Rahman: do we get trace links back to our app logs? we need to correlate request ids from the app to redwood traces.

[07:59] Diego Alvarez: yes, we accept a client-provided request_id header and will echo it in every trace. if your agent strips headers, we can also provide a small SDK snippet that pushes a correlation id.

[08:15] (screen shows CPU/GPU metrics tied to trace)
[08:28] Diego Alvarez: the console couples serving runtime metrics to the request trace so you can see device saturation at the time of the call. that's often the smoking gun for intermittent tail latency.

[08:45] Samir Gupta: about private deployments — if we go Private behind a customer VPC, is there still a control plane that sends traces to Redwood? we need local-only telemetry.

[08:58] Priya Nair: we support a private control plane mode where telemetry can be stored locally and a pared-down control-plane endpoint communicates only metadata. for fully air-gapped installs there's an on-prem package — telemetry never leaves your network unless you opt in.

[09:20] Maya Thompson: quick qualification: what's your timeline for pilot and who signs off on security?

[09:28] Aisha Rahman: timeline is 2-4 weeks to run a pilot, security will need SOC2 docs and a network diagram, and product will validate the replay and trace fidelity. cost is secondary but we want to understand unit economics if we scale to 1000 req/s.

[09:50] Diego Alvarez: noted. we'll include a cost baseline plus a recommended batching and cache configuration to hit 1000 rps targets.

[10:05] (Diego drills into an incident view)
[10:15] Diego Alvarez: here's a complex incident where requests were intermittently misrouted during an autoscaling event. Timeline shows: spike in inbound QPS, autoscaler spun new pods, some pods didn't warm KV-cache, initial requests experienced cache miss waterfall, app retried and hit fallback model. console shows a 'retry storm' pattern and suggests three mitigations: increase pre-warm batch size, enable prefix caching, and set a graceful queueing window.

[10:48] Liam Chen: pre-warm? we haven't implemented pre-warm across our instance types. will that require code changes?

[10:56] Diego Alvarez: minimal — you can configure pre-warm policies at the deployment level or use the SDK warmup call. for some customers we run an autoscaler hook that triggers a synthetic warmup sequence.

[11:12] Nora Patel: curious about the rollback play — can we run A/B compare and automatically roll back if quality drops?

[11:21] Priya Nair: yes, rollouts support canary with automatic rollback based on evaluation metrics. the console evaluates quality regressions against a ground-truth prompt set and can be configured to rollback if metric drift exceeds thresholds.

[11:40] Maya Thompson: showing the Eval Lab briefly — you can attach a prompt set and baseline outputs; the system will surface precision/recall-like metrics and token-level deltas.

[11:55] Aisha Rahman: does the console expose model artifacts so we can run offline evals? we prefer to pull weights into our private infra for offline tests.

[12:06] Diego Alvarez: we don't export model weights for hosted customers, but for Dedicated/Private deployments we provide model bundles and quantization profiles that you can run locally. note: licensing and compliance discussions apply.

[12:28] (Short pause as screens change)
[12:40] Diego Alvarez: back to traces — i'm going to show the 'stitch graph' where multiple partial traces from microservices get merged. it uses heuristics: header-based correlation, approximate timestamp alignment, and event-name matching. occasionally names collide and we surface ambiguous matches for manual review.

[13:05] Liam Chen: how often do ambiguous merges happen? we worry about false positives.

[13:12] Diego Alvarez: depends on instrumentation fidelity. with full SDK tracing it's rare; with sidecar-only capture it's higher. we include a confidence score per merge and you can set a threshold to refuse low-confidence merges.

[13:30] (Diego pulls up logs view)
[13:38] Diego Alvarez: logs view supports redaction rules — you can define regexes to strip PII before the log is stored. we also support streaming to your SIEM with an optional buffer for burst durability.

[14:02] Samir Gupta: does the console do differential debugging — like show diffs between two runs at token level?

[14:10] Diego Alvarez: yes, the side-by-side diff highlights tokens with probability shifts and annotates any decoding anomalies. we also show a quality delta and a suggested root cause like 'tokenization mismatch' or 'quantization artifact'.

[14:35] Nora Patel: can we script replay batches? we have a backlog of 12k failing requests.

[14:42] Diego Alvarez: there's an API and CLI for batch replays. you submit a job, it runs on bench infra, and we stream progress back to the console. for large runs you may want to limit concurrency to manage cost.

[15:00] (Diego shows an export popup)
[15:08] Diego Alvarez: exports — you can export full trace JSONs, a flattened CSV of spans, or a sanitized artifact for compliance.

[15:20] Aisha Rahman: will you share a simple run-book for our on-call to triage these incidents?

[15:28] Maya Thompson: yes we'll include a tailored run-book that covers triage steps: correlate request ids, check KV cache state, replay, compare outputs, and then escalate to model team if needed.

[15:40] (Customer asks a deep technical question)
[15:45] Samir Gupta: KMS integration detail — does Redwood support customer-managed keys in cloud KMS and HSM-backed key policies? and are trace logs encrypted at rest with those keys?

[15:58] Priya Nair: yes to both. we support CMEK in AWS/GCP/Azure and HSM-backed keys for dedicated/private. traces and logs can be encrypted under your key; access requests are logged in audit trail.

[16:18] Liam Chen: what about SSO and RBAC? our org uses SAML and enforces least privilege.

[16:26] Maya Thompson: we support SAML SSO with fine-grained RBAC, you can create roles that only allow replay or only allow read-only traces. we'll send a sample SAML metadata file in the follow-up.

[16:40] (Diego opens a troubleshooting checklist)
[16:48] Diego Alvarez: quick troubleshooting checklist in the console: 1) check correlation IDs, 2) inspect KV-cache hit rate, 3) check device metrics at call time, 4) run a replay and compare logits, 5) escalate with the logs + replay artifact.

[17:12] Nora Patel: if we want to run replays in our private infra, can we use the console UI or will it be CLI-only?

[17:20] Priya Nair: if you're private on-prem we provide a console package that runs behind your network and gives full UI parity. some customers opt to run headless and use the CLI for automation.

[17:38] Maya Thompson: wrapping up, do you have any objections or blockers to a pilot?

[17:44] Aisha Rahman: main blockers: SOC2 artifacts and a network diagram for security review, plus we want to guarantee that test replays won't leak data.

[17:54] Samir Gupta: also need clarity around retention: default vs private deployment.

[18:01] Maya Thompson: we'll send SOC2 + data flow diagram and include retention defaults and configuration options.

[18:08] Diego Alvarez: one last demo snippet — automated alert rules: you can set up a regression alert that triggers on token-level KL divergence or an unexpected spike in fallback rate. it can kick off a replay job automatically.

[18:30] Liam Chen: automation would be huge. can the alert create a ticket in jira?

[18:36] Diego Alvarez: yes, has integrations: Slack, PagerDuty, Jira, webhook.

[18:45] (wrap up)
[18:50] Maya Thompson: thanks all. we'll follow up with the security pack, run-book, and a proposed pilot plan. any final Qs?

[19:02] Aisha Rahman: no, that's good. thanks everyone.

End notes: demo lasted ~58 minutes including Q&A. Several specific follow-ups and pilot prerequisites agreed.

(Transcript may include occasional mislabels and auto-parsed names; some timestamps approximate.)
